title: The Sterile Stomach
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, a patient with a peptic ulcer, a raw crater in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum just beyond it, was told a story about acid and nerves, with coffee, alcohol, tobacco, and spicy food cast as accomplices.
In 1910 the surgeon Karl Schwarz compressed that story into a maxim, "no acid, no ulcer," and for seventy years it held.
In 1915 the Chicago physician Bertram Sippy prescribed hourly feedings of milk and cream to soak up the stomach's acid.
When rest and diet failed, surgeons cut the vagus nerve to reduce acid output or removed part of the stomach.
The theory produced one genuine triumph.
In 1976 the pharmacologist James Black and his colleagues introduced cimetidine, which blocks the histamine receptors on the stomach's acid-making cells and so turns acid production down.
Ulcers that had festered for years healed within weeks, and Black shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine partly for this work.
Yet the triumph had a hollow center.
Cimetidine healed ulcers but did not cure the disease: once the drug was stopped, most ulcers returned within a year, and many patients simply took it indefinitely.
One reason nobody looked for a germ was that everybody knew the stomach was sterile: its contents can reach a pH below 2, and acid that strong kills most bacteria quickly.
In the 1890s the Italian pathologist Giulio Bizzozero described spiral organisms in the stomachs of dogs, and others later reported similar shapes in human stomachs.

But in 1954 the American gastroenterologist Eddy Palmer examined more than a thousand stomach biopsies, found no bacteria in any of them, and concluded that the earlier sightings were contamination from the mouth.
His stains, it was later noted, were not the silver stains that show the organisms best, but his conclusion was what the field expected, and it stuck.
The sighting that mattered came from Perth, in Western Australia.

In 1979 Robin Warren, a pathologist at Royal Perth Hospital, noticed curved bacteria in a biopsy from an inflamed stomach, and with a silver stain he kept finding them, always in the mucus near the surface cells and always beside inflamed tissue.
In 1981 Barry Marshall, a trainee in internal medicine looking for a research project, joined him.

Together they examined biopsies from 100 consecutive patients and found the bacteria in nearly every patient with active gastritis, the inflammation that precedes an ulcer, and nearly every patient with a duodenal or gastric ulcer.
Patients whose stomach lining was normal seldom carried them.
Seeing the organism was one thing; growing it was another.
For months Marshall tried to culture it, treating it like Campylobacter, a known gut bacterium of similar shape, and routine called for discarding any plate that showed nothing after two days.
Over the Easter weekend of 1982 a batch of plates was left in the incubator for five days instead, and when it was checked, tiny colonies had appeared.
The organism was simply slow.
It was spiral, bore several whip-like flagella at one end, and grew only in air with reduced oxygen, a requirement microbiologists call microaerophilic.

It was first named Campylobacter pyloridis, after the pylorus, the muscular outlet where the stomach empties into the duodenum; in 1989, once it was clearly a genus of its own, it became Helicobacter pylori, the helical bacterium of the pylorus.
How does it live where nothing was supposed to live?
The answer is an enzyme called urease, which the bacterium makes in abundance.
Urease splits urea, a waste compound present in gastric juice, into ammonia and carbon dioxide, and the ammonia neutralizes the acid in a small cloud around each cell.
Protected this way, the bacterium swims through the thick mucus that coats the stomach lining and settles against the surface cells, where the pH is close to neutral.
The medical world did not rush to agree.
In 1983 the Gastroenterological Society of Australia rejected Marshall's summary of the findings, and a presentation abroad met with open skepticism.
The objections were serious ones.

The stomach was sterile, so the organisms were probably contaminants; the bacteria might simply be colonizing tissue that something else had damaged, so correlation was not cause; and the germ, it soon became clear, lived in many people with no ulcer at all.
Behind the arguments, I suspect, stood something less rigorous: a profitable industry built on acid suppression, and a profession that had learned its ulcer theory as settled fact.
Warren and Marshall's full paper, in The Lancet in 1984, concluded cautiously that the bacterium might be an important factor in the diseases.
Marshall chose to answer the causation objection the oldest way.

In the 1880s the German bacteriologist Robert Koch had set out the tests for blaming a microbe for a disease, now called Koch's postulates: find it in every case, grow it in pure culture, produce the disease by giving it to a healthy host, and recover it from that host.
The organism had been found and grown; the third step required a healthy host, and attempts to infect laboratory animals had failed.
So in 1984, after an endoscopy confirmed that his own stomach was healthy, Marshall drank a culture of the bacterium taken from a patient.
Within about a week he was nauseated and vomiting, and a biopsy on the tenth day showed a stomach lining crowded with the organism and acutely inflamed.
After two weeks he took antibiotics and recovered; the account appeared in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1985.
I admire the nerve and distrust the method.

One volunteer who develops gastritis but no ulcer, which is what happened, does not prove that the germ causes ulcers; it showed that the organism could colonize a healthy stomach and inflame it, and that made the question impossible to dismiss.
What settled the matter was duller and better: clinical trials.
Through the late 1980s and early 1990s, groups in Perth, Houston, Vienna, and elsewhere gave ulcer patients antibiotics, with or without acid suppression, and followed them for a year or more.
The pattern was consistent: ulcers healed with acid suppression alone came back in most patients within a year, while ulcers in patients whose bacteria had been eradicated almost never returned.

In 1994 a consensus panel convened by the National Institutes of Health concluded that ulcer patients carrying the bacterium should receive antibiotics, and later that year the World Health Organization's cancer agency classified it as a cause of stomach cancer.
It would be satisfying to say the old theory was simply wrong, but the truth is more tangled, and more interesting.
Acid still matters.

When the bacterium settles in the antrum, the lower part of the stomach, it disturbs the hormonal signals that regulate acid and drives output up, which is one reason ulcers form downstream in the duodenum.
Schwarz's maxim was right about the mechanism and silent about the cause.
Nor is the germ the only culprit: aspirin and related painkillers damage the stomach lining directly, and most ulcers in people free of the bacterium are traced to those drugs.

Most puzzling of all, the bacterium infects roughly half the people on Earth, usually from childhood and usually for life, yet most carriers never develop an ulcer; lifetime estimates run between one in ten and one in five.
In 2005 Warren and Marshall shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the bacterium and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
The organism was not hiding; it had been seen in the 1890s, and anyone with a silver stain and a stubborn disposition could have found it in 1954.
What hid it was a sentence everyone could recite, and a treatment that worked just well enough to keep anyone from asking why the disease kept coming back.
Consensus is not evidence, and a theory that explains the mechanism of a disease has not necessarily found its cause.

The story is usually told as two outsiders against the establishment, and that is true as far as it goes, but I would put it differently: the establishment was not stupid, it was merely finished, and a finished question is the most dangerous kind.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Bertram Sippy's treatment for ulcers consisted of
choices: cutting the vagus nerve to lower the stomach's output of acid
hourly feedings of milk and cream to soak up stomach acid
a drug that blocks histamine receptors on acid-making cells
removing the lower part of the stomach, where acid is produced
antibiotics combined with a drug that suppresses stomach acid

proof.quote: Bertram Sippy prescribed hourly feedings of milk and cream to soak up the stomach's acid

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says it directly: in 1915 Sippy prescribed hourly feedings of milk and cream to soak up the stomach's acid. The surgery and the drugs belong to other people and other years.
distractorNotes: Wrong treatment: paragraph 1 gives the vagus nerve to surgeons, not to Sippy.
Wrong paragraph: the histamine blocker is cimetidine, introduced by James Black in paragraph 2.
Wrong treatment: removing part of the stomach was the surgeons' last resort, and nothing says acid is made in the lower part.
Wrong era: antibiotics with acid suppression are the trials of paragraph 9, decades after Sippy.

questions.stem: The author describes cimetidine in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: argue that acid suppression should be abandoned as a treatment for ulcers
show that James Black deserved his Nobel Prize more than Warren and Marshall did
explain the chemistry by which histamine triggers the stomach's acid-making cells
present the acid theory's greatest success and expose its limit
introduce the clinical trials that later compared antibiotics with acid suppression

proof.quote: The theory produced one genuine triumph.
Cimetidine healed ulcers but did not cure the disease

questions.why: Paragraph 2 opens by calling cimetidine the theory's one genuine triumph and closes by saying it healed ulcers but did not cure the disease. The drug is there to show how far the acid theory could go and where it stopped.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 10 says acid still matters, so the author never argues for abandoning acid suppression.
Outside the passage: the author never compares the two prizes or ranks the winners.
Not the purpose: the paragraph names the receptor in passing and explains no chemistry.
Wrong paragraph: the trials arrive in paragraph 9, and paragraph 2 does not mention them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Eddy Palmer concluded in 1954 that
choices: earlier sightings of stomach bacteria were contamination from the mouth
spiral organisms lived in the stomachs of dogs but not of humans
silver stains were too unreliable to detect bacteria in biopsies of the stomach
the stomach's acid was not strong enough to kill most bacteria
biopsies had to be examined within hours or any bacteria would die

proof.quote: concluded that the earlier sightings were contamination from the mouth

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Palmer examined more than a thousand biopsies, found no bacteria, and concluded that the earlier sightings were contamination from the mouth.
distractorNotes: Mash-up: the dogs belong to Bizzozero in the 1890s, and others reported the shapes in humans too.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says Palmer did not use silver stains, not that he judged them unreliable.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says acid that strong kills most bacteria quickly, which is why the stomach was thought sterile.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about how quickly biopsies had to be examined.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'sterile' most nearly means
choices: unable to produce offspring
lacking imagination or vitality
cleaned with heat or chemicals
barren and unproductive
free of living microbes

proof.quote: everybody knew the stomach was sterile: its contents can reach a pH below 2, and acid that strong kills most bacteria quickly

questions.why: Paragraph 3 explains the word in the same sentence: the acid kills most bacteria quickly, so sterile here means free of living microbes.
distractorNotes: This is the reproductive sense of the word, and nothing in the sentence concerns offspring.
This is the figurative sense, as in a sterile debate, and the sentence is about acid and bacteria.
This describes a process done to instruments; the stomach is not cleaned, it is simply too acidic for microbes.
This is the sense used of land or soil, and the sentence is about germs, not productivity.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if Palmer had used a silver stain in 1954, he would most likely have
choices: found the bacteria only in patients who already had ulcers
confirmed that the organisms Bizzozero saw were oral contaminants
seen the organisms in at least some of the biopsies he examined
cultured the organism decades before Marshall managed to
been believed, since the field was ready for a new theory

proof.quote: were not the silver stains that show the organisms best
anyone with a silver stain and a stubborn disposition could have found it in 1954

questions.why: Paragraph 3 notes that Palmer's stains were not the silver stains that show the organisms best, and paragraph 11 says outright that anyone with a silver stain could have found the bacterium in 1954. With the right stain, some of his thousand biopsies would have shown it.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 4 finds the bacteria in gastritis as well as ulcers, and paragraph 10 says half the world carries it.
Reversed: a stain that shows the organisms would have undercut the contamination explanation, not confirmed it.
Wrong step: a stain makes organisms visible under a microscope; growing them on plates is the separate problem of paragraph 5.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says his conclusion stuck because it was what the field expected, so a new finding would have met resistance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Warren and Marshall's study of 100 patients, the bacteria were
choices: present in nearly every patient who had active gastritis or an ulcer
present in every patient, including those whose stomach lining was normal
found only in patients with duodenal ulcers, not in those with gastric ulcers
cultured successfully from the biopsies of most of the patients
seen in dogs as well as in humans, confirming Bizzozero's report

proof.quote: found the bacteria in nearly every patient with active gastritis, the inflammation that precedes an ulcer, and nearly every patient with a duodenal or gastric ulcer

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the bacteria turned up in nearly every patient with active gastritis and nearly every patient with a duodenal or gastric ulcer, while patients with normal stomach lining seldom carried them.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 4 says patients with normal stomach lining seldom carried the bacteria.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 names duodenal and gastric ulcers together.
Wrong paragraph: this study was about seeing the bacteria in biopsies; culturing came later and is the subject of paragraph 5.
Wrong paragraph: the dogs belong to Bizzozero in paragraph 3, and this study examined only human patients.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the organism was finally cultured in 1982 because
choices: Marshall stopped treating it like Campylobacter and changed the growth medium
the incubator was set to a lower oxygen level over the holiday
the biopsies were taken from patients with ulcers rather than gastritis
a batch of plates was left in the incubator longer than routine allowed
the laboratory began using silver stains to check the plates for colonies

proof.quote: a batch of plates was left in the incubator for five days instead, and when it was checked, tiny colonies had appeared

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says routine called for discarding plates after two days, but over Easter 1982 a batch sat for five days, and that was when colonies appeared. The organism was simply slow.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 5 says he was treating it like Campylobacter, and no change of medium is mentioned.
Mash-up: the bacterium does need reduced oxygen, but paragraph 5 credits the extra time, not a change in the incubator.
Outside the passage: nothing links the breakthrough to which patients the biopsies came from.
Wrong paragraph: silver stains are for seeing bacteria in tissue (paragraphs 3 and 4), not for checking plates.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage as features of Helicobacter pylori EXCEPT:
choices: It has a spiral shape.
It carries flagella at one end.
It grows only in air with reduced oxygen.
It makes the enzyme urease in abundance.
It grows quickly on culture plates.

proof.quote: It was spiral
bore several whip-like flagella at one end
grew only in air with reduced oxygen
which the bacterium makes in abundance
The organism was simply slow.

questions.why: Paragraph 5 gives the shape, the flagella, and the reduced-oxygen requirement, and paragraph 6 gives the urease. The one thing the passage says the opposite of is speed: the organism was simply slow, which is why two-day plates showed nothing.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 5: it was spiral.
Stated in paragraph 5: several whip-like flagella at one end.
Stated in paragraph 5: it grew only in air with reduced oxygen.
Stated in paragraph 6: the bacterium makes urease in abundance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, urease protects the bacterium by
choices: thickening the mucus layer that coats the stomach lining
producing ammonia that neutralizes the acid around each cell
breaking down the acid itself into carbon dioxide and water
lowering the pH at the surface cells to a level the bacterium tolerates
propelling the bacterium through the mucus toward the surface cells

proof.quote: the ammonia neutralizes the acid in a small cloud around each cell

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, and the ammonia neutralizes the acid in a small cloud around each cell.
distractorNotes: Wrong role: the mucus is the stomach's own coating, and paragraph 6 never says the enzyme changes it.
Wrong chemistry: paragraph 6 says urease splits urea, not acid, and the products are ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Reversed: lowering pH means more acid; the enzyme's ammonia makes the surroundings less acidic.
Wrong part: swimming through the mucus is the job of the flagella in paragraph 5, not of an enzyme.

questions.stem: The author lists the objections in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: demonstrate that the skeptics had misread the Lancet paper
show that the scientific community was motivated purely by profit
grant that the doubters had real arguments before suggesting other motives
explain why Marshall's summary was rejected by the society in 1983
prepare the reader for the clinical trials that would answer each objection in turn

proof.quote: The objections were serious ones.
Behind the arguments, I suspect, stood something less rigorous

questions.why: Paragraph 7 introduces the list by calling the objections serious ones, and only after laying them out does the author add, I suspect, that something less rigorous stood behind them. The list gives the skeptics their due before the author's own suspicion.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the Lancet paper is mentioned after the objections, and nothing says the skeptics misread it.
Too strong: the author calls the objections serious and offers profit only as a suspicion, not the whole explanation.
Half right: the rejection is mentioned earlier in the paragraph, but the list is about why the field doubted, not about one society's decision.
Wrong paragraph: the trials in paragraph 9 settle the question overall; they are not matched to each objection in turn.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Marshall's self-experiment fell short of fulfilling Koch's third postulate for ulcers because
choices: he never confirmed his stomach was healthy before drinking the culture
the bacterium he swallowed had been grown from a laboratory animal rather than a patient
he took antibiotics before the organism could be recovered from him
no endoscopy was performed until after the symptoms had already cleared
the disease the postulate required, a peptic ulcer, never developed in him

proof.quote: produce the disease by giving it to a healthy host
One volunteer who develops gastritis but no ulcer, which is what happened, does not prove that the germ causes ulcers

questions.why: Paragraph 8 states the third postulate as producing the disease in a healthy host, and then says Marshall developed gastritis but no ulcer. For ulcers, the disease in question never appeared, so the step was not completed.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 8 says an endoscopy confirmed his stomach was healthy before he drank the culture.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the culture was taken from a patient, and animals could not be infected at all.
Contradicted: the biopsy on the tenth day found the organism before he took antibiotics after two weeks.
Contradicted: the tenth-day biopsy showed a lining crowded with the organism and acutely inflamed, so it came during the illness.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Marshall's self-experiment is best described as
choices: admiring yet doubtful
openly contemptuous
coolly indifferent
wholly approving
bewildered and dismissive

proof.quote: I admire the nerve and distrust the method.
does not prove that the germ causes ulcers

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says it in one line: I admire the nerve and distrust the method. The author then explains why one volunteer proves little while still crediting the experiment with keeping the question alive.
distractorNotes: Too harsh: an author who admires the nerve is not contemptuous.
Too cool: the author takes a clear position and argues it in two directions.
Half right: the admiration is there, but the author also distrusts the method and says the experiment proved little.
Wrong register: the author explains exactly what the experiment did and did not show, with no confusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the clinical trials of the late 1980s and early 1990s showed that
choices: antibiotics healed ulcers faster than acid suppression did
ulcers treated with antibiotics alone returned in most patients within a year
ulcers seldom returned once the bacteria had been eradicated
acid suppression was unnecessary once antibiotics were given
patients in Perth, Houston, and Vienna responded differently to treatment

proof.quote: ulcers in patients whose bacteria had been eradicated almost never returned

questions.why: Paragraph 9 gives the pattern: ulcers healed with acid suppression alone came back in most patients within a year, while ulcers in patients whose bacteria had been eradicated almost never returned.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the trials measured whether ulcers came back, and paragraph 9 says nothing about speed of healing.
Reversed: it was acid suppression alone that led to relapse in most patients.
Too strong: paragraph 9 says antibiotics were given with or without acid suppression and never calls acid suppression unnecessary.
Reversed: paragraph 9 says the pattern across the groups was consistent.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that cimetidine failed to cure ulcers because it
choices: was taken for too short a time to heal the crater completely
lowered acid without removing the organism that drove the disease
blocked histamine receptors on the bacterium rather than on the stomach cells
thickened the mucus layer in which the bacterium lives
suppressed acid so completely that the bacterium spread more easily

proof.quote: Cimetidine healed ulcers but did not cure the disease
ulcers healed with acid suppression alone came back in most patients within a year, while ulcers in patients whose bacteria had been eradicated almost never returned

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says cimetidine healed ulcers but did not cure the disease, and paragraph 9 explains the difference: acid suppression alone led to relapse, while eradicating the bacteria did not. Put together, the drug treated the acid and left the cause in place.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 says ulcers healed within weeks, and many patients took the drug indefinitely.
Wrong target: paragraph 2 says the receptors are on the stomach's acid-making cells, not on any bacterium.
Outside the passage: nothing says cimetidine changes the mucus.
Outside the passage: no link between acid suppression and the spread of the bacterium is ever made.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Helicobacter pylori infection EXCEPT:
choices: It is found in roughly half the people on Earth.
It is usually acquired in childhood.
It usually lasts for life.
It leads to an ulcer in most carriers.
It can drive the stomach's acid output up.

proof.quote: infects roughly half the people on Earth
usually from childhood
usually for life
drives output up
most carriers never develop an ulcer

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the bacterium infects roughly half the people on Earth, usually from childhood and usually for life, yet most carriers never develop an ulcer, with lifetime risk between one in ten and one in five. The acid rise comes earlier in the same paragraph.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 10: roughly half the people on Earth.
Stated in paragraph 10: usually from childhood.
Stated in paragraph 10: usually for life.
Stated in paragraph 10: in the antrum it disturbs the hormonal signals and drives acid output up.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 11?
choices: A homeowner whose basement floods each spring pumps it dry every time and never asks where the water comes from
A gardener whose roses keep wilting tests the soil, finds a fungus, and treats the roots before replanting them
A coach benches a star player after one bad game, certain that the player's talent has suddenly vanished
A pilot rechecks the fuel gauge before every flight even though it has never once given a false reading
A student memorizes the answers to last year's exam and is surprised to fail this year's entirely different test

proof.quote: a treatment that worked just well enough to keep anyone from asking why the disease kept coming back
a theory that explains the mechanism of a disease has not necessarily found its cause

questions.why: Paragraph 11's principle is that a fix which manages the mechanism well enough can stop anyone from asking about the cause. Pumping out the water every spring is cimetidine; never asking where it comes from is the ulcer field before Warren and Marshall.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the gardener hunts for the cause and treats it, which is what the ulcer field failed to do.
Wrong principle: this is a hasty judgment from one event, not a working fix that hides a cause.
Wrong principle: this is caution about a problem that has never occurred, with nothing recurring and nothing hidden.
Wrong principle: this is a failure to prepare for something new, not a recurring problem patched over without asking why.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Barry Marshall's self-experiment was the decisive proof that bacteria cause peptic ulcers
The acid theory of ulcers was a mistake that delayed effective treatment for seventy years
A settled theory kept medicine from seeing the bacterial cause of ulcers that was in plain view
Peptic ulcers are now cured with antibiotics because Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach's mucus
Warren and Marshall succeeded because they ignored the scientific establishment entirely

proof.quote: One reason nobody looked for a germ was that everybody knew the stomach was sterile
The organism was not hiding
What hid it was a sentence everyone could recite
Consensus is not evidence

questions.why: The passage opens with a theory everyone could recite, shows that the organism had been seen and ignored, follows the discovery through to the trials, and closes by saying that what hid the germ was consensus itself. Only one choice carries both the discovery and the lesson.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the self-experiment proved little, and paragraph 9 says the clinical trials settled the matter.
Too strong: paragraph 10 says acid still matters and that Schwarz's maxim was right about the mechanism.
Too narrow: the mucus and the antibiotics are details from paragraphs 6 and 9, not the argument of the whole passage.
Outside the passage: they published in The Lancet and presented to the societies; nothing says they ignored the establishment.
